title: Part 1 Practice: Concepts, Features, and Significance of IKS

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a term used to refer to Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS)?
options: A) Folk knowledge.
B) Local knowledge.
C) Non-formal knowledge.
D) Western scientific knowledge.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) is called after different but closely related names, which include: 'folk knowledge', 'local knowledge', 'non-formal knowledge', 'cultural knowledge', 'indigenous technical knowledge', 'traditional ecological knowledge', and 'traditional knowledge'.' Western scientific knowledge is a separate system.

questions.text: According to Mangetane (2001), what is Indigenous Knowledge (IK)?
options: A) A theoretical knowledge system from universities.
B) Technical insight of wisdom gained through years of careful observation and experimentation in a particular locality.
C) A purely written body of knowledge.
D) A static set of beliefs.
questions.correct_answer: B) Technical insight of wisdom gained through years of careful observation and experimentation in a particular locality.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Mangetane (2001) defined IKS as technical insight of wisdom gained and developed by people in a particular locality through years of careful observation and experimentation with the phenomena around them.'

questions.text: What is a defining feature of Indigenous Knowledge regarding its transmission?
options: A) It is transmitted through written textbooks.
B) It is transmitted orally, or through imitation and demonstration.
C) It is transmitted only through the internet.
D) It is transmitted through legal documents.
questions.correct_answer: B) It is transmitted orally, or through imitation and demonstration.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Transmitted orally, or through imitation and demonstration. Although codifying IK is generally possible, care should be taken since codifying it may lead to the loss of some of its properties.'

questions.text: What does it mean that IK is 'tacit' knowledge?
options: A) It is written in books.
B) It is not explicit or codified; it is carried and transferred through practices, myths, rituals, and symbols.
C) It is purely theoretical.
D) It is universally applicable.
questions.correct_answer: B) It is not explicit or codified; it is carried and transferred through practices, myths, rituals, and symbols.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'The tacit nature of IK suggest that people may develop and carry knowledge and transfer it between generations using practices, myths, rituals and symbols... but may not be able to articulate them equivalent to scientific categories.'

questions.text: What are the two main purposes for which socio-cultural anthropologists study IKS?
options: A) For political gain and economic profit.
B) For the sake of understanding local knowledge as an end in itself, and for the sake of application to solve development challenges.
C) Only for academic publishing.
D) Only to preserve ancient texts.
questions.correct_answer: B) For the sake of understanding local knowledge as an end in itself, and for the sake of application to solve development challenges.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Socio-cultural Anthropologists study IKS for two main purposes. First, anthropologists study IKS for the sake of understanding local peoples' knowledge as an end by itself... Second, Socio-cultural Anthropologists study IKS for the sake of application.'

questions.text: According to the World Development Report (1998/99), what is the key to sustainable social and economic development?
options: A) Physical capital.
B) Knowledge, not capital.
C) Military power.
D) Natural resources.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'According to the 1998/99 World Development Report, knowledge, not capital, is the key to sustainable social and economic development.'

questions.text: What was the success rate of rural water projects when indigenous knowledge was incorporated, compared to when it was not?
questions.explanation: The module states: 'a study of 121 rural water projects in 49 countries found that 70 percent succeeded when the intended beneficiaries participated (indigenous knowledge incorporated) in project design, compared to a 10 percent success rate among programs where they did not.'

questions.text: What does it mean that Indigenous Knowledge is 'dynamic'?
options: A) It is static and never changes.
B) It is produced as well as reproduced, discovered as well as lost, and constantly changes.
C) It is only about the past.
D) It is fixed in written form.
questions.correct_answer: B) It is produced as well as reproduced, discovered as well as lost, and constantly changes.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Constantly changing, that is, IK is not static. Rather IK is dynamic in its nature. It is produced as well as reproduced, discovered as well as lost.'

questions.text: What are the socio-economic values embedded in IKS?
options: A) Only profit and wealth.
B) Values related to intergenerational relationships, gender equality, tolerance, hospitality, reciprocity, and hard work.
C) Only political power.
D) Only religious beliefs.
questions.correct_answer: B) Values related to intergenerational relationships, gender equality, tolerance, hospitality, reciprocity, and hard work.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'Socio-economic Values: Values related to intergenerational relationships, gender equality, tolerance for diversity, interpersonal relationships and respectfulness, hospitality, reciprocity, and interdependence, values for productivity, wealth, and hard work.'

questions.text: According to the module, how can IKS and scientific knowledge be used together?
options: A) They cannot be combined.
B) IKS can be used as an alternative, or combined with scientific knowledge to create culturally appropriate and environmentally sustainable solutions.
C) Scientific knowledge should always replace IKS.
D) IKS should only be used in isolation.
questions.correct_answer: B) IKS can be used as an alternative, or combined with scientific knowledge to create culturally appropriate and environmentally sustainable solutions.
questions.explanation: The module states: 'IKS can be used for application in two main ways. On one hand, it can be used as an option or alternative to scientific or Western knowledge systems... On the other hand, where appropriate, we can combine indigenous and Western knowledge systems.'
